description: Duquesne University professor among the Americans who died in flooding in Nepal  CBS News
publisher.title: CBS News
full_article:
The Duquesne University community is remembering a professor who died in the deadly flooding and mudslides in Nepal earlier this year.

Dr. Mark Cantrell was 51 years old and taught in the John G. Rangos School of Health Sciences.

"Dr. Cantrell's work in public health, global health security, and health systems took him to all parts of the globe as he strove to improve access to high-quality health care for many different populations," a statement from the university said. "His work in diplomacy, with USAID, with the United Nations, and numerous other agencies not only was admirable but also provided our students context and insights that will continue to inform and inspire how they think about their own work serving others."

Former students remembered Dr. Cantrell as approachable and lighthearted, while colleagues said his passion for public health took him around the world.

Dr. Cantrell died while returning to Nepal following a spiritual pilgrimage.

Duquesne University has not yet announced plans for a memorial service or any other observances, but in a letter to the entire university, it said it will share those when they become available.

title: No ground, no game: Why Nepal’s football dream is dying at grassroots? - The Rising Nepal
description: No ground, no game: Why Nepal’s football dream is dying at grassroots?  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
BY BIBEK SHRESTHA,Kathmandu, Sept. 20: FIFA World Cup 2026 concluded a few months ago, with Spain lifting their second title since 2010. During the tournament, fiery discussions could be heard across various social media platforms regarding Nepal’s failure to qualify for the world’s biggest sporting stage. Pundits frequently compared Nepal with other qualifying nations such as DR Congo, Senegal, Cape Verde and Haiti. At some point, the comparisons seemed justified given the economic parallels.

Countries with lower nominal GDPs and smaller populations participated in the World Cup. Nepal’s nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) stands at approximately $45.84 billion, whereas Senegal’s stands at $40.47 billion, and Haiti, a Caribbean nation, reports a nominal GDP of around $39 billion. Meanwhile, DR Congo delivered a remarkably commendable campaign despite severe domestic turbulence. Cape Verde, an island nation of approximately 530,000 people, was the favourite underdog, challenging some of the tournament’s favourites. Fans and critics asked a poignant question: if nations wrestling with acute social, political and economic crises can qualify, why can’t Nepal?

Much of the discourse has rightfully targeted at the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA), framing institutional mismanagement as the root cause of the country’s sporting decline. While administrative failures have undoubtedly crippled Nepali football, public debate consistently omits a crucial factor: community football. In many African and Caribbean nations, grassroots football is followed with religious devotion. Despite political instability, gang violence and soaring inflation, local communities actively foster young talent, building a resilient foundation from the ground up. Despite lacking strong domestic leagues, these nations have both the space and willingness to encourage young players who play their professional football in Europe’s top-flight leagues.

In Nepal, community football, local club tournaments and grassroots academies—the very incubators meant to nurture young talent—have all but vanished. Over the past two decades, rapid migration and unchecked urbanisation have swallowed the Kathmandu Valley’s open spaces, leaving major cities suffocating under concrete congestion. According to the 2021 National Population and Housing Census, the population of Kathmandu district alone surpassed two million. In such an urban bottleneck, where are children supposed to play, run and fall in love with the game?

“Football used to be ubiquitous; most importantly, it didn’t cost money. I still have vivid recollections from my childhood; my brother and I would wake up early in the morning and go for training,” said Jitendra Nepali, who played football for local club National Amity Youth Club in the early 2010s and even got exposure in C Division. He sighed: “We would have plenty of open space to play, unrestricted fields to cherish the game. We didn’t have to pay, and that was the most inspiring factor, but now, everything has changed.”

When he realised that pursuing his passion would go in vain as Nepal’s Martyr’s Memorial A-Division League was suspended following corruption scandals, he took a different turn in his life and started working as a cook to support his family. He shared his concerns for today’s children about how their fundamental right to play has been violated and worries about his own children’s upbringing.

Prabesh Bista, who has been in the United States pursuing higher education, vividly remembers the passionate football culture of his childhood a decade ago. “I grew up in Manamaiju, where we never had to worry about open fields because there were plenty,” he recollected. “Yet, we still had to queue for our turn because there were so many players.”

Now returning to Nepal every two years, Bista is struck by the dramatic transformation of his old neighbourhood.

Where public fields once stood, commercial futsal venues have sprung up in tightly squeezed pockets of urban space. These private facilities charge around Rs. 1,500 per hour for recreational play, with premium locations commanding even higher rates. In the vicinity of Manamaiju and Tarkeshwor Municipality alone, there are now nearly 15 privately owned futsal courts, yet hardly a single open, free public ground remains.

While venue owners and former professional players running futsal academies view this expansion as a positive evolution for local sports, some critical questions are routinely ignored: how many neighbourhood children can afford Rs. 1,500 a day just to play the game they love? Children belonging to higher-income families may have the capacity to afford it, but can a child belonging to a lower-middle-class family struggling to make ends meet afford to train at these academies or play at these futsal courts?

Bookings are mostly occupied by adults over 40; one can hardly see children playing at futsal courts every day. Aarush Neupane, a Grade 9 student who currently resides in Kalanki, one of the core areas of the capital, said, “Every weekend, my classmates and I book futsal. Since we don’t have public fields, we are compelled to play at futsal courts that charge even higher at weekends.” He shared the sobering reality that they collect their lunch money and pay the futsal court charges because they love the game.

As commercial competition intensifies across Nepal’s private education sector, schools are locked in a social media arms race—touting lavish amenities to attract prospective parents. Among the most coveted selling points are state-of-the-art futsal courts. However, behind the polished promotional videos lies a stark disconnect between advertised infrastructure and campus reality.

For many urban families, modern sports facilities serve as a primary decision-making factor during admissions. Yet, students report that these high-cost infrastructures often function more as decorative billboards and social media content than accessible sports resources.

“Most private schools have futsal courts these days,” said Niraj Giri, a Grade 9 student. “Parents enrol their children, lured by these facilities, but the irony is that students are not even permitted on the court, and there are no instructors to train us.”

Nepal celebrated Constitution Day on September 19, marking the 11th anniversary of the promulgation of the Constitution of Nepal in 2015. Although Article 39, Clause (2) explicitly guarantees every child the right to education, health, maintenance, proper care, sports, entertainment and overall personality development from the family and the State, urban children remain systematically deprived of these opportunities amid severe congestion and unplanned urbanisation. Constitutional rights are not meant to remain confined to paper; they must be actively implemented for the holistic development of children and, ultimately, the progress of the nation itself.

The government demolished almost 20,000 squatter structures from the banks of the Bishnumati River in May. These newly vacated spaces could potentially be utilised for community football and other recreational activities in a city where even an acre of vacant land is increasingly difficult to find. Rather than allowing such spaces to remain unused, authorities could consider developing accessible community sports grounds, particularly for children and young people who have few affordable places to play.

When public spaces vanish, children’s passion for sports dies along with them. When local clubs such as National Amity Youth Club are fighting for their survival, local football, local tournaments and the crucial exposure young talents need to flourish disappear along with them. Before a nation can ever dream of playing on the world stage, its children must first have a place to fall in love with the game.

The fall of Nepali football did not start at the top. It began in our neighbourhoods.

title: Constitution Day puts Nepal’s constitutional future in focus - The Kathmandu Post
description: Constitution Day puts Nepal’s constitutional future in focus  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal marked the 11th anniversary of its constitution on Saturday with political leaders calling for its core achievements to be protected while differing over how the charter should evolve.

President Ramchandra Paudel called for full implementation of the constitution, while Prime Minister Balendra Shah said his government was committed to upholding it in both letter and spirit. Leaders of major political parties, however, placed varying emphasis on constitutional review, possible amendments and translating its guarantees into improvements in people’s daily lives.

The constitution, promulgated on September 20, 2015, established a federal democratic republic and enshrined fundamental rights, inclusive and proportional representation and a federal system of government.

Addressing a Constitution Day ceremony at the President’s office in Sheetal Niwas, Paudel said the constitution had laid the foundation for civil liberties, the rule of law, inclusive representation and social, cultural and economic transformation.

He called for full compliance with its provisions, greater accountability in public administration, more effective constitutional bodies and easier access to justice.

“Democracy will be strengthened only when we establish a culture of respecting disagreement, learning from criticism and making the state accountable to the people,” Paudel said.

The head of the state said the constitution should be viewed not simply as a written document but as a shared commitment to citizens’ aspirations, expectations and rights.

This year’s Constitution Day is marked as Nepal deals with the aftermath of the devastating Bhotekoshi flood of August 26. President Paudel called for a united effort to provide relief, rescue and rehabilitation to those affected, while stressing the need for transparent, accountable and results-oriented government.

At a separate ceremony at Tundikhel, Prime Minister Shah said the government was committed to implementing the constitution and its underlying principles.

“However good a constitution may be, it becomes a piece of paper if those entrusted with implementing it are not honest and continuously active,” Shah said. “This is the beginning, not the end.”

He said the government’s priorities included ending discrimination and inequality, promoting development and prosperity, and building a more equitable society based on social justice.

Shah also highlighted good governance, saying the government was working to reduce the size of the administrative machinery, maintain zero tolerance for corruption, ensure political neutrality in the bureaucracy and make appointments to public and state positions on the basis of merit.

The government, he said, was also committed to cooperation and coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments.

Shah linked constitutional implementation with economic and technological change, saying his government was working towards a knowledge-based economy centred on artificial intelligence, digital technology, cybersecurity, innovation and startups.

“Good governance is not a slogan,” Shah said. “It is work.”

While the President and prime minister focused largely on implementation and governance, party leaders used Constitution Day to outline different priorities for the next phase of the charter.

Ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party chair Rabi Lamichhane described the constitution as a “sacred contract” between the state and citizens.

He said its fundamental rights would have meaning only when they became part of the daily lives of marginalised citizens. Nepal still has work to do to build a stronger foundation for economic prosperity, social justice and good governance, he said.

Lamichhane also called for a review of the constitution centred on people at the margins of society.

“The constitution is a living document,” he said. “Its provisions can evolve and be amended based on experience gained through political practice.”

Nepali Congress president Gagan Kumar Thapa said constitutional amendments should be discussed with “courage and clarity” while protecting the charter’s basic values and principles.

He said years of political practice had exposed weaknesses that should be addressed through amendments aimed at strengthening democratic values.

Former prime minister and chairman of CPN-UML KP Sharma Oli, meanwhile, emphasised protecting the constitution and strengthening national unity. He called on forces supporting the constitution to stand together to safeguard it.

Former prime minister and coordinator of Nepali Communist Party Pushpa Kamal Dahal said the immediate task was to connect the achievements of the constitutional process with people’s lives and complete the remaining work.

Political change, he said, should be linked to improvements in education, healthcare, employment, production and equal opportunities.

Former prime minister Baburam Bhattarai also argued for amendments, but stressed the need to preserve the federal democratic republic, secularism, federalism and inclusive democracy.

Speaking to the state-run news agency, Rastriya Samachar Samiti, on the occasion, Bhattarai said amendments should be pursued through national consensus and build on the democratic gains already made.

He cautioned against making fundamental changes in anger or haste, saying such an approach could put existing achievements at risk.

The differing messages reflect a broader debate over Nepal’s constitutional experience after 11 years.

There is broad political recognition of the importance of the federal democratic system, fundamental rights and inclusive representation. The disagreement is over what should come next: stronger implementation of existing provisions, institutional reform, a broader review or targeted constitutional amendments.

For Paudel, the immediate challenge is to make the constitutional system more accountable and effective. For Shah, it is to turn its principles into governance and public policy. Lamichhane has called for a review centred on marginalised citizens, while Thapa has argued for amendments to address weaknesses exposed by practice. Oli has stressed protection and national unity, and Dahal has focused on connecting constitutional achievements with people’s everyday lives.

The debate comes as Nepal continues to grapple with questions about the effectiveness of its federal institutions, delivery of public services, governance and the implementation of constitutional rights.

title: Nepal fails to agree on scope of constitutional reform — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal fails to agree on scope of constitutional reform — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the government of Balendra Shah has failed to secure the support of parliamentary parties in preparing changes to the 2015 Constitution. A working group formed after the government’s decision of March 30, 2026, submitted its report on July 16, but the document has still not been made public. As the Kathmandu Post reports, the report proposes amending 245 of the Constitution’s 308 articles — nearly 80% of the document.

Parties’ distrust of the initiative

The scale of the potential changes has raised concerns among political forces that participated in drafting and adopting the fundamental law. The Nepali Congress, Communist Party of Nepal — Unified Marxist-Leninist, Nepal Communist Party, and several Madhesh-based parties questioned the government’s purpose, asking whether it was seeking amendments or an effective rewriting of the Constitution.

The Nepali Congress refused to delegate a representative to the working group. A representative of the Communist Party of Nepal — Unified Marxist-Leninist boycotted its meetings, while representatives of other parties that initially joined the discussions later withdrew from the process.

The group’s coordinator, Asim Shah, a political adviser to the prime minister, said it had not been tasked with drafting amendments directly. According to him, the report is intended to serve as reference material for a future commission tasked with preparing constitutional changes and includes all proposals received during consultations. They include restoring a constitutional monarchy, revising the model of state governance and the electoral system, introducing an executive president, and changes to the functioning of independent constitutional bodies.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Barrier in parliament

Amendments require the support of two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers of the federal parliament. The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party holds nearly two-thirds of seats in the lower house but has no representation in the National Assembly. An amendment to the House of Representatives’ rules had previously been proposed that would calculate two-thirds of votes jointly across both chambers. The Supreme Court suspended it, finding it unconstitutional.

Constitutional expert Bipin Adhikari believes that the government’s lack of transparency and the absence of a clear position on the specific provisions it plans to review hinder a substantive discussion. Another expert, Chandra Kanta Gyawali, stressed the need to assess problems identified over the Constitution’s 11 years in force.

Positions on the future model

The Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal — Unified Marxist-Leninist advocate preserving the parliamentary model, republican system, and mixed electoral system, while allowing limited administrative adjustments. The Nepal Communist Party and Janata Samajbadi Party Nepal support direct elections for the head of the executive and a fully proportional electoral system. The Rastriya Prajatantra Party seeks the restoration of a constitutional monarchy and a Hindu state.

At the same time, most parties agree on the need to clarify the division of powers among the federal, provincial, and local levels of government, reduce the number of local units, and cut the size of provincial assemblies and cabinets. Asim Shah said the government plans to first advance changes on which a nationwide consensus can be reached.

title: Can ‘Mission 2026’ finally deliver Nepal its first Asian Games gold? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Can ‘Mission 2026’ finally deliver Nepal its first Asian Games gold?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
In 18 appearances at the Asian Games, Nepal’s tally stands at 26 medals—23 bronze, three silver and zero gold.

When the 20th Asian Games officially opened in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday, 40 of the 135-member Nepali contingent from 21 sports marched into the Paloma Mizuho Stadium behind flag-bearers Chandra Bahadur Thapa and Manmati Bist with an audacious goal: reach double-digit medals and bring home the country’s first-ever gold from the continental flagship event.

It is a dream born out of both desperation and design.

Two decades ago, at the 15 th Asian Games in Doha, Qatar, in 2006, taekwondoins Deepak Bista, Ayasha Shakya and Manita Shahi secured three bronze medals for Nepal. At the time, karate legend Deepak Shrestha issued a grim warning: without long-term, systemic preparation, Nepal would struggle to stay competitive as rival nations poured millions into sports infrastructure.

His words proved prophetic. For the next three editions, Nepal won only one medal in each edition—a boxing bronze by Deepak Maharjan in Guangzhou 2010, a karate bronze by Bimala Tamang in Incheon 2014, and a paragliding team silver in Jakarta-Palembang 2018—often relying more on individual grit and luck than state strategy.

The narrative shifted slightly at the delayed 2022 Hangzhou Games, which was held in 2023 due to Covid-19, where karateka Erika Gurung clinched historic silver, and the women’s kabaddi team bagged bronze. The double-medal finish prompted the National Sports Council to announce ‘ Mission 2026 ’—a long-term plan promising uninterrupted training, dietary support and adequate exposure for top athletes.

Now, as competition begins in Nagoya, ‘Mission 2026’ faces its final exam.

“Based on the preparation and performance metrics we’ve tracked, we are expecting results that match our effort,” said Deepak Shrestha, who now serves as the director of national team preparation under the National Sports Council. “With the form Erika has maintained, we are firmly expecting a medal haul that includes at least one gold.”

Yet, Shrestha admits the journey to Nagoya was plagued by familiar bureaucratic hurdles. Budget shortfalls earlier this year temporarily disrupted national camps, forcing coaches and sports associations to scramble.

“Government bodies and sports federations treated ‘Mission 2026’ as if it was purely the NSC’s private project,” Shrestha lamented. “When funds ran short, training was derailed, and no one else stepped up. We cannot rely on paper plans alone. But now that we are here, we must convert that preparation into podium finishes.”

Nepal’s highest medal hopes rest on combat sports—karate, boxing, wushu and taekwondo—alongside women’s kabaddi. There would have been hopes for some more medals had the e-sports athletes not been denied participation despite qualifying for the 20 th Asian Games.

Gurung, whose silver in Hangzhou revitalised Nepali martial arts, remains the country’s brightest gold prospect. Her coach, Kushal Shrestha, expressed supreme confidence ahead of Gurung’s first match against Yara Naser of Jordan in the quarterfinal of the women’s kumite +68kg on Sunday.

Sanu Maya Thing, who is also expected to bring home a medal, is up against Haeun Choi of South Korea in women’s individual kata’s Round of 16. Gurung and Thing will compete at Toyohashi Gymnasium.

In boxing, flag-bearer Chandra Bahadur Thapa enters the ring on Monday backed by a historic bronze medal performance at the 2025 IBA Men’s World Boxing Championships. Manmati Bist leads a women’s kabaddi squad aiming to upgrade their Hangzhou bronze.

Unlike previous editions where Nepal sent bloated contingents largely for participation’s sake, the roster in Aichi-Nagoya has been slashed by nearly half compared to Hangzhou. Only 135 athletes across 21 sports made the cut following strict internal selection criteria.

The decline of once-dominant sports is also evident. Taekwondo, which historically anchored Nepal’s Asian Games tally, has shrunk to just three athletes in Nagoya—Abhishek Baral in the men’s -80kg category, alongside Yubraj Rana and Swastika Tamang in Poomsae via wildcard entries.

title: Nepali Flood Message and Condolences from Mayor Jake Wilson - The Somerville Times
description: Nepali Flood Message and Condolences from Mayor Jake Wilson  The Somerville Times
publisher.title: The Somerville Times
full_article:
Three weeks ago, flash floods devastated communities along the China-Nepal border, but the sheer scale of this nightmare is still revealing itself. Rescuers are desperately searching for the over 6,150 people still missing, while over 1,400 lives have been confirmed lost.

Survivors of the floods are facing a difficult recovery. In an instant, an area filled with vibrant communities, just like Somerville, was decimated. The infrastructure impacts are catastrophic, with $200 million needed to repair Nepal’s roads and bridges alone. But the personal losses are immeasurable. It’s estimated that the floods destroyed 8,317 Nepali homes. That’s thousands of tables where families gathered for meals, thousands of beds parents used to tuck in their kids – vanished in seconds.

But we can help. If you’re able to support recovery efforts, donations can be made to the Nepali Red Cross or directly to the Government of Nepal through the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund. There’s a long road to recovery ahead for Nepal, but with our support, survivors don’t need to walk it alone.

I also want to share my gratitude and sympathy with Somerville’s Nepali community. Over the past three weeks you’ve transformed your grief and fear into the type of courage and resilience that is an inspiration and call to action for all of us.

Longtime Somerville resident Vijendra Kumar Pradhan, who recently passed, exemplified that spirit. My deepest condolences on this profound loss are with his family, friends, and the entire Nepali community. Vijendra was a talented artist, energetic community leader, and cherished friend to many. He served as President of the Newah Organization of New England and was an impactful member of the Greater Boston Nepali community. His generosity, friendship, and kindness now serve as lights to help guide all of us through these difficult times.

-Mayor Jake Wilson

title: Meaningful Employment - The Rising Nepal
description: Meaningful Employment  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
As Nepal embarks on a new chapter of social and economic change, the country’s youth face a challenge that is more than a search for employment. For millions of young Nepalis, the search is no longer just about earning a living; it is increasingly about finding meaningful employment that offers dignity, stability, personal growth and a sense of purpose.

Nepal has one of the youngest populations in South Asia, with a large percentage of its citizens in the working age group. This demographic dividend can be the engine of national development, innovation and economic growth. But the lack of enough quality jobs has forced many young people to rethink their future in the country. Every year, thousands of youths leave Nepal in search of better opportunities abroad.

For many families, foreign employment has emerged as a key source of income. However, the increasing trend of migration of skilled and educated young people has raised concerns about Nepal’s ability to utilise its own human resources. Many graduates are having difficulty finding employment in areas related to their qualifications. Instead, they often accept low-paid, temporary or unrelated jobs due to a lack of opportunities in the domestic market.

“The problem is not that young people do not want to work; the problem is that they want work that is suitable for their skills and ambitions”, said an employment expert in Kathmandu. Young Nepalis today are seeking careers where they can contribute creatively, grow professionally and be secure in the long term, rather than just survive from one opportunity to another.

Technology and entrepreneurship are opening up new possibilities for some young people. Digital platforms, freelancing, start-ups and online businesses have opened up alternative career options. Young entrepreneurs are establishing businesses in sectors like information technology, agriculture, tourism, education and creative industries. These examples show that Nepal's youth are not short of talent or ambition; they need better support systems, investment and opportunities.

However, youth employment is still constrained by several barriers. One of the biggest challenges is the gap between education and industry needs. While the government and private sector have come up with various employment and skill development programmes, many of the youth say these need to be better implemented and made more accessible. Career guidance, vocational training, digital skills development and support to small businesses could make a big difference in preparing youth for changing labour markets.

Meaningful employment also means creating workplaces where young people feel valued and appreciated. The younger generation is increasingly searching for good pay, career opportunities, safe working conditions and appreciation of employees’ efforts. There are many youths willing to work hard, but they want careers that are in line with their personal values and future goals.

Experts say Nepal’s future depends a lot on how well it can engage its young population. A push for education reform, entrepreneurship, technology and sustainable industries could turn Nepal’s youth population into a powerful force for national development. Ultimately, Nepal’s youth’s search for meaningful employment is a search for hope and possibility. Young Nepalis are not shirking responsibility; they are looking for opportunities where their skills, creativity and commitment can help build a better tomorrow. Now, it is up to the policymakers, businesses and society to provide Nepal’s greatest resource, its youth, a reason to stay, grow and succeed in the country.

title: Nepal-China Ecological Cooperation - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal-China Ecological Cooperation  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
The mighty Himalayas along the Nepal-China border symbolise their deep bonhomie and shared ecological destiny, not elements of division. The snowy mountains, glaciers, and lakes straddle both countries, implying that they are bound by the Himalayan ecosystem. If any disaster occurs on the common border, it hits them equally. The Bhotekoshi flash flood affirms this fact. It was triggered by a glacial collapse at the Nepal-China border. Both countries suffered a huge loss of life and infrastructure. This catastrophe has brought Nepal and China together to minimise the risks. This has necessitated ecological cooperation between them, as the global warming-induced climate change has posed an existential threat to the planet.

Like in the past, China has once again proved an age-old adage - a friend in need is a friend indeed. In the aftermath of the flood, China immediately sent essential relief supplies and equipment to expedite the search, rescue and relief work conducted by Nepali security agencies. It provided $ 2.4 million, five batches of aid relief supplies, drones, Bailey bridges, and DNA testing equipment, among others. Altogether, 24 Chinese experts on tunnel rescue, DNA identification and forensic identification came to Nepal to ease rescue operations and support post-disaster management.

Fighting misinformation

The two countries need to counter misinformation, disinformation, rumours, and conspiracy theories aimed at undermining their relations. Evidence-based narratives, scientific facts, and robust communication help counter misleading information that spreads through social media during natural disasters. For instance, after the Bhotekoshi flood pounded the downstream communities, baseless rumours that ‘China did not provide early warning’ and ‘China sent the flood’ made the rounds. Those unable to sift the fact from disinformation subscribed to the claims. However, it is noted that hundreds of Chinese people have also lost their lives in the tragedy caused by the glacier collapse. Unfortunately, unfounded heresies are circulated during the time of calamities, grief and confusion.

However, Chinese sources have said that there has been constant communication on transboundary disaster management between the two nations. The Chinese embassy has said that Chinese expert teams have made every effort to conduct monitoring, assessment and analysis and have shared important information with the Nepali side promptly. Its statement came in response to an allegation that China failed to inform Nepal about the possibility of a mudslide disaster in time. The embassy also pointed to the limits of technology to conduct ground surveys of a large number of glaciers and ice-rock masses situated at an elevation of 4,000 to 5,000 metres or above. Image errors on steep slopes and high-precision monitoring over vast and complex terrains remain international challenges, it said.

In an interview given to this daily recently, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal stated that the two countries have been in communication regarding the situation of glacial lakes located on the Nepal-China border. In August, a team from the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment of the Chinese Academy of Sciences visited Nepal to exchange China's practical experience in glacial lake monitoring. The China Meteorological Administration has provided Nepal with preliminary customised services under the "MAZU", the Chinese Intelligent Meteorological Early Warning Solution, enhancing the two countries' capacity to respond to transboundary disasters, according to the embassy. In May this year, a delegation from the Ministry of Water Resources of China and the Department of Water Resources of Xizang Autonomous Region visited Nepal and made substantial progress with the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority of Nepal to set up a transboundary disaster information-sharing mechanism. On August 26, the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology of Nepal held a virtual meeting with the China Meteorological Administration to assess the disaster situation and share data simultaneously. Chinese Ministry of Water Resources said that it would continue to share information on risks of barrier and glacial lakes and emergency hydrological monitoring with Nepal.

Fighting climate change has become a shared responsibility as it is not confined to a particular country. In the past, Western industrial nations used excessive fossil fuels and sent large amounts of carbon dioxide into the air. China is a latecomer in industrial development. The greenhouse gas emissions accumulated over centuries are now melting the Himalayas. So blaming a particular country will complicate Nepal’s bid for climate finance. It will be a grave diplomatic faux pas to seek climate justice compensation from any specific country, including China. Nepal has already initiated a claim for reparation from the international community within the framework of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and its Paris Agreement.

Sound ties

Nepal and China enjoy excellent ties in the fields of diplomacy, politics, defence, trade, tourism, culture, education and so on since they established diplomatic relations in 1955. Both have inked several bilateral agreements and memoranda of understanding. With the flurry of activities, people-to-people contact has grown over the decades. Both are now working to implement development projects to realise the Nepal-China Trans-Himalayan Multi-Dimensional Connectivity Network and cross-border railway connectivity. The agreement on the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has become a milestone in giving impetus to connectivity, investment, technology transfer, trade and cultural bonds. In 2019, their relations were elevated to a strategic partnership during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Nepal.

Now, climate cooperation has become an indispensable subject in Nepal-China bilateral activity. They need to forge an ecological partnership, with a focus on environmental resilience and climate security. There should be no delay in constituting the joint mechanisms to ensure real-time satellite data-sharing, joint meteorological forecasting and early-warning networks between the two nations. China is a powerful voice in international forums. It is also the second-largest mandatory contributor to the UN budget. It should leverage its influence in helping Nepal access climate funds.

(The author is the Managing Editor of this daily.)

title: Nepal takes its message to the world - Nepali Times
description: Nepal takes its message to the world  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah is making his first foreign trip to speak at the United Nations General Assembly on 24 September, and just about everyone everywhere is giving him advice about what he should say.

Going by the content of the PM’s address to the nation and social media posts since the 26 August disaster, climate justice will be right at the front and centre of his delivery. Assigning blame for the climate crisis will, no doubt, be a compelling message during the year of a super-charged El Niño. It will also add counterweight to rising climate denialism and rollback on decarbonisation by populist flat-earthers.

Nepal’s annual per capita carbon footprint is 0.5 tons – only 0.1% of total global emissions. The annual per capita carbon footprint of the United States is 15 tons and is second only to China, but China has a much smaller per capita footprint. The US and other industrialised states are also responsible for historical release of carbon dioxide, the greenhouse gas that stays in atmosphere for hundreds of years.

Global average temperature is already 1.5°C above the pre-industrial baseline, and a phenomenon called ‘elevation-dependent warming’ means the Himalaya is heating up 0.7°C faster. The average temperature on the north side of Langtang Lirung in the week preceding the rock slide was 5°C at 5,200m elevation – the highest ever recorded in the area.

The Bhote Kosi-Trisuli Flood was not unexpected, scientists have been warning of even worse events. This is a global warning about warming. It is not just a Nepal disaster, but presages what is coming for the planet and life on it.

For three weeks, the global media was focused on the Trisuli. Terrifying videos of the debris flow burying towns set off a wave of sympathy for Nepal, with an outpouring of humanitarian aid. But the attention span of the international media lasts only some weeks before it moves to other hotspots.

Nepal is already falling off the map, and needs to capture the moment. When Prime Minister Shah walks up to the General Assembly podium it will have been exactly a month since the China-Nepal flood. What he says there, how he says it, and how it is received will determine whether Nepal’s soft power has disproportionately more clout than the country’s size and economic importance.

VICTIM CARD

It will be tempting for Nepal to play victim, and make the industrialised world guilty about historical emissions. We have the evidence and moral high ground to assign such blame. The international community will commiserate and offer platitudes, but one thing is clear -- empty empathy is not cash.

The Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment published by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has put the cost of this disaster at $4.7 billion. The Fund has a $20 million disbursement cap on claims, so why extend our arms for alms from an entity that has no money?

Besides, the Fund’s funders have set strict criteria for deciding what constitutes a ‘climate disaster’. This is like the police asking a bruised and battered victim of a mugging to get written proof that he was mugged. Fund managers will point to geotectonic factors in the 26 August disaster, and trolls will call us ‘grifters’.

Instead, let us highlight our contributions: doubling forest area to 46% in the past 30 years, most of our electricity is hydro, and 75% of new vehicles are EVs (page 5). We can say: “This is what we have done. What have you done?”

There is evidence that permafrost melting due to record high temperatures fractured the bedrock on which the ice shelf rested on Langtang. The slope collapse was only a small part of a huge mountain. Multiply Langtang by hundreds of other massifs in Nepal and southern Tibet and it is clear 26 August is a warning of even bigger Himalayan tsunamis.

Climate breakdown may have been only one factor in the Langtang rock-ice collapse, but future outburst floods from thousands of expanding glacial lakes in Nepal and China could add to the threat of even more catastrophic cascading and compounding hazards.

Nepal has only itself to blame for allowing settlements along floodplains, and locating a dozen hydropower plants on a single basin. This disaster was a wakeup call for Nepal to build back safer not just in the Trisuli Valley but also along other rivers (page 1), and to figure out how to pay for climate resilience and damage in the future (page 10-11).

Next week at the UN General Assembly, Nepal’s prime minister will alert the world: look at what happened to us, it will happen to you unless we all stop pumping more greenhouse gases into the air.

Kunda Dixit
